analysis.one_liner: Gives every child a $1,000 federal savings account, paid for by higher taxes on large estates and capital gains.
analysis.headline: Cory Booker's bill to create government-funded savings accounts for children died in the Senate Finance Committee with no cosponsors and never received a vote before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would open a federally managed savings account for every American child, seeded with $1,000 at birth and topped up each year on a sliding scale — up to $2,000 a year for families below the poverty line, tapering to nothing for households above five times the poverty line. The money could only be spent on education, buying a home, or held for retirement, and would not count against eligibility for other federal benefits. To pay for it, the bill raises the estate tax to as much as 65% on the largest estates, cuts the tax-free estate exemption to $3.5 million, raises the capital gains rate to 24.2%, and taxes unrealized gains when someone dies or gives assets away.
analysis.who_benefits: Children, weighted heavily toward those in low- and middle-income households. A child in a family under the poverty line would receive $1,000 at birth plus $2,000 every year until 18, plus interest; contributions shrink on a sliding scale and reach zero for households above five times the poverty line.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children in low- and middle-income families

how_it_helps.text: Every eligible child gets a $1,000 account at birth, with annual contributions of up to $2,000 for households at or below the poverty line, sliding down to zero for households above 500% of the poverty line.
Account funds may only be withdrawn for qualified expenses: education, ownership of a home, expenses after age 59½, or other investments the Treasury approves as building long-term wealth.

Balances in the accounts would be ignored when determining eligibility for any federally funded benefit, including student financial aid, so the savings would not cost a family food stamps or Pell Grants.
Contributions, earnings, and distributions from the accounts would be excluded from federal income tax.

analysis.who_pays: The bill is funded entirely by taxes on concentrated wealth: the top estate tax rate rises to 45%, with rates of 55% on estates over $10 million and 65% over $50 million; the basic exclusion drops to $3.5 million; the capital gains rate rises to 24.2%; and unrealized capital gains are taxed as a sale when someone dies or gifts assets away, with a $100,000 exclusion (and a $1 million exclusion for qualifying farm property).
analysis.who_pays_short: Large estates and wealthy asset holders

drawbacks.text: The program is a permanent new federal entitlement: the Treasury must transfer $1,000 per child at birth plus annual payments for roughly 18 years for every child born after 2018, paid from general tax revenue and the new taxes, with no sunset provision.

The fund must invest exclusively in 30-year U.S. Treasury debt, so the accounts would earn government bond returns rather than the higher average returns of a diversified stock portfolio, reducing the balances children eventually receive.
The benefit phases in only for children born after December 31, 2003, so today's adults and even many teenagers would get little or nothing from the program for well over a decade.

Taxing capital gains as a sale at death could force heirs of illiquid assets — a family business, for example — to sell property to pay the tax, though the bill softens this with a 15-year installment option, a $100,000 exclusion, and $1 million for qualifying farm real property.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a large, well-targeted wealth-building program: the money flows to children, weighted toward the poorest households, and comes from the estates of the very wealthiest families. The real tradeoffs are a permanent multi-billion-dollar annual federal cost, modest investment returns because the fund is limited to Treasury bonds, the long lag before any child sees a payout, and the administrative complexity of taxing gains at death. Critics would also object on principle to a government-managed account for every child in place of private savings.

outcome.mechanism: Booker introduced the bill in the Senate's final days and it was referred to the Finance Committee, which never considered it, and the 115th Congress ended with no cosponsors and no vote.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the American Opportunity Accounts Act on December 18, 2018, during the closing days of the 115th Congress.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance; that referral is the last action in its history.
The Senate adjourned for the end of the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019, without the Finance Committee taking any action or the Senate voting on the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy families with large estates, big unrealized capital gains, and trust-based estate planning keep the existing tax rules — the 40% estate tax with a much larger exemption and no tax on gains at death — which the bill would have raised substantially.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the American Opportunity Accounts Act on December 18, 2018.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on December 18, 2018 and took no further action — no markup, no report, no vote.

against.name: Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration during the committee's final weeks.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, and no vote was ever taken, so there is no roll-call record; the Republican-chaired Finance Committee simply declined to act.

industries.industry: Largest estates and holders of appreciated assets
industries.note: The bill raises the estate tax to as much as 65% on estates over $50 million, cuts the exemption to $3.5 million, raises the capital gains rate to 24.2%, and taxes gains as a sale at death or gift. Their tax bill is the program's funding source.

The bill cracks down on techniques used to pass wealth untaxed: it requires grantor retained annuity trusts to run at least 10 years with a large minimum remainder, and pulls grantor trust assets back into the taxable estate. These strategies are the core product of high-end estate planning.

The bill raises the special farm real property valuation limit from $750,000 to $3 million and adds a $1 million exclusion for qualifying farm property at death, but only for land actually used for farming, with a 10-year recapture tax if the heir sells or converts it. Farms still face the new tax on gains at death above those carve-outs.
